title: 7.8.2 Lab: Waves
description: Enemies stop arriving on a beat and come in waves instead: each wave only after the field is clear and a pause has run out, each one bigger and faster. Write nextWave and spawnWave, and start every round at wave 0.

steps.title: A round starts at wave 0
steps.instructions: `spawnOnBeat()` is gone: enemies now come in waves. The top of the screen says `wave: undefined`, running into `base:` beside it, because nothing sets the wave yet. In `startRound()`, set `wave` to 0 and `wavePause` to 60, so every round, the first one and every one after R, starts with a one-second pause before wave 1. Run it: the top should read `wave: 0`.
hints: `wave = 0;` and `wavePause = 60;`, beside the other lines that put a round back.
`startRound()` is called by `setup()` and by the R key, so one place covers both.

steps.title: Count down on a clear field
steps.instructions: In `nextWave()`, return straight away while any enemies are left. Otherwise count `wavePause` down by 1, and when it reaches 0 call `spawnWave()` and set `wavePause` back to 90. This is 7.8.1's `nextWave()`, word for word.
hints: The countdown is Part A's cooldown under another name: take 1 off every frame, and act at 0.

steps.title: Build a wave
steps.instructions: In `spawnWave()`, add 1 to `wave` and set `fallSpeed` to `0.5 + wave * 0.25`, so each wave falls a little faster. Then loop `wave + 2` times. On loop number `i` the enemy is tough (3 hp) when `i % 3 === 2` and has 1 hp otherwise; build it with `spawnEnemy(40 + floor(random(8)) * 45, -20 - i * 50, hp)`, which stacks the wave above the top in a staggered line, each at a random spot across the screen. Play to wave 3, then press R in the middle of a wave: the field should empty, `wave:` should read 0, and wave 1 should come again after the pause.
hints: `const hp = i % 3 === 2 ? 3 : 1;` makes every third enemy a tough one.
`-20 - i * 50` puts each enemy 50 pixels above the one before it, so they come down one after another.

requirements.title: Every round starts at wave 0 with a pause
requirements.description: startRound sets wave to 0 and gives wavePause a number of frames (a number, or a named constant). Help: 7.8.1 (Worked Example: Waves with a pause)

requirements.title: The pause counts down only on a clear field
requirements.description: nextWave counts wavePause down by 1 only on a clear field: it returns while any enemies are left, as 7.8.1 does (or, as in 7.3.18, starts a wave only when the field is clear on a frameCount beat). Help: 7.8.1 (Worked Example: Waves with a pause)

requirements.title: At 0 the next wave comes and the pause starts again
requirements.description: When wavePause reaches 0, nextWave calls spawnWave() and sets wavePause back to a number above 0 (or a named constant). Help: 7.8.1 (Worked Example: Waves with a pause)

requirements.title: A wave adds 1 to the wave number and builds its enemies in a loop
requirements.description: spawnWave adds 1 to wave and calls spawnEnemy inside a loop. Help: 7.8.1 (Worked Example: Waves with a pause)

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code
aiCheck.prompt: The student wrote a moSHion sketch (p5-style JavaScript with a physics world) for the lab "7.8.2 Lab: Waves". The task they were given: Enemies now come in waves. In startRound(), set wave to 0 and wavePause to 60. In nextWave(), return straight away while any enemies are left; otherwise count wavePause down by 1, and when it reaches 0 call spawnWave() and set wavePause back to 90. In spawnWave(), add 1 to wave, make each wave fall a little faster than the last, and loop wave + 2 times, building each enemy with spawnEnemy(...), every third one a tough one with 3 hp. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do when the sketch runs. moSHion facts that matter here: setup() runs once; draw() runs about 60 times a second, and so does every function it calls. kb.presses('space') is true only on the one frame a key goes down; kb.pressing('space') is true on every frame it is held. y grows downward. In this game draw() calls the game's own functions every frame, inside if (playing) { ... }. sprite.delete() (its other name is remove()) takes a sprite off the screen, and array.splice(i, 1) takes it out of the array; a shot or enemy that is gone has to leave both the screen and the array. A loop that runs from the end of an array to the start never skips an item when one is spliced out. overlaps() asks whether two sprites touch right now and changes nothing; it works for sprites with collider 'none', and colliding() never sees such a sprite. drawTop() runs after the sprites are drawn, so its words sit on top; text drawn in draw() lands underneath the sprites. The enemies live in three parallel arrays, enemies (the sprites), enemyHp and enemyWorth: index j in all three is the same enemy, so every push and every splice has to happen to all three at the same index, or every later enemy reads a neighbour's numbers. A helper such as removeEnemy(j) that deletes the sprite and splices all three counts wherever it is called, as if its lines were written there. startRound() runs from setup() and from the R key, so it is the one place a round's numbers start again. draw() calls nextWave() every frame while playing. return inside a function ends that function for this frame. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable, parameter and helper-function names, template strings, arrow functions, a ternary or an if/else chain, x++ or x += 1 or x = x + 1, semicolons, spacing, quotes and order are all fine. Names that other code in the program already calls (startRound, nextWave, spawnWave, spawnEnemy) must keep those names, because a renamed one is never called. Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment or a string never runs, and the STEP comments the starter came with are not the student's work. The starter's three places are only STEP comments: missing on every criterion. The exact numbers for speed, hp, positions and wave size are asked by the steps but are not criteria. Write each note for THIS student's own code, for a 14-year-old reader: short sentences, plain words. In a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.

rubric.title: Every round starts at wave 0 with a pause
rubric.description: startRound() sets wave to 0 and gives wavePause a number of frames above 0 (60 in the step; any number or a named constant). Setting them only in setup() is not met: R would not reset them. Leaving wavePause unset is not met: the countdown could never reach 0.

rubric.title: The pause counts down only on a clear field
rubric.description: nextWave() takes 1 off wavePause only while no enemies are left: an early return while enemies.length is above 0, or the countdown inside an if that asks the list is empty. Starting a wave only on a clear field on a frameCount % beat (the 7.3.18 shape) also counts. A countdown that runs while enemies are still falling is not met.

rubric.title: At 0 the next wave comes and the pause starts again
rubric.description: When wavePause reaches 0 (<= 0, === 0, or < 1), nextWave() calls spawnWave() and sets wavePause back to a number above 0 (or a named constant). Never setting wavePause back is not met: after the first wave a new one would start on every clear frame. With the 7.3.18 frameCount beat instead, calling spawnWave() inside that clear-field beat counts.

rubric.title: A wave adds 1 to the wave number and builds its enemies in a loop
rubric.description: spawnWave() raises wave by 1 (+= 1, ++, or = wave + 1) and calls spawnEnemy(...) inside a for or while loop, so the number of enemies can grow with the wave. Calling spawnEnemy a fixed number of times by hand, with no loop, is partial.
